title: Senior's toolkit: charts that ship
summary: The matplotlib object API, saving charts that look right in a report, pandas and seaborn plotting, and closing figures in scripts.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: charts that ship
steps.body: A chart for a report has to be labelled, sized and saved the same way every run, often from a script. Experienced analysts use matplotlib's figure-and-axes API for that, with pandas or seaborn drawing onto those axes.

toolkit.what: Create a figure and its axes explicitly, then call methods on `ax`. Clearer and safer than the global `plt.plot` state once there is more than one chart.
flags: a grid; `axes` is then an array
the same scale on every panel, so they compare honestly
toolkit.example: fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True, layout="constrained")

toolkit.what: Set the title, axis labels and limits in one call. A chart without units on its axes is not finished.
flags: start the y axis at zero for bars
toolkit.example: ax.set(title="Daily revenue", xlabel="Date", ylabel="Revenue (GBP)", ylim=(0, None))

toolkit.what: Save the chart for a report or a slide.
flags: sharp enough for slides and print
crop to the content, so labels are not cut off
the extension picks the format; SVG scales without blur

toolkit.what: pandas plots straight from a DataFrame, using the index as x. Pass `ax=` to draw on the axes you created.
flags: draw on this panel instead of a new figure

toolkit.what: Statistical charts from a tidy DataFrame in one line, also onto your `ax`. Good for distributions and group comparisons.
Free a figure when a script makes many of them. Figures stay in memory until closed.
toolkit.example:
for store, g in df.groupby("store"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    g.plot(x="day", y="sales", ax=ax)
    fig.savefig(f"{store}.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)

steps.prompt: The PNG you attach to the weekly report has its y-axis label and the bottom of the date labels cut off, though it looks fine in the notebook. What fixes it?
options: Save with `bbox_inches="tight"` (or create the figure with `layout="constrained"`)
Shorten the label to one letter
steps.explain: Notebooks crop the display for you; `savefig` uses the figure's exact size unless told to fit the content. More dpi only makes the cut-off parts sharper.

steps.prompt: A script draws one chart per store, 300 stores. It prints `RuntimeWarning: More than 20 figures have been opened` and memory keeps climbing. What is missing?
options: Running it in a notebook instead
steps.explain: pyplot keeps every figure alive until it is closed, so a loop that never closes them leaks memory. Close each one as soon as it is saved.

steps.prompt: You made `fig, axes = plt.subplots(ncols=2)`, then called `daily.plot()` and `weekly.plot()`. Both appear in two new figures, and your side-by-side figure is empty. What is the fix?
steps.explain: Without `ax=`, pandas makes a new figure. Passing the axes is what lets you build multi-panel figures with pandas, seaborn and matplotlib together.

steps.prompt: Two panels side by side with the same y scale, pandas drawing on the first, saved without cropping problems.
code: fig, axes = plt.subplots(__1__=1, ncols=2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True)
steps.explain: `nrows`/`ncols` set the grid, `ax=` picks the panel, and `bbox_inches="tight"` crops to the content when saving.

steps.prompt: Match each argument to its effect.
pairs: the same y scale on every panel
labels spaced so they do not overlap

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Start every chart with `fig, ax = plt.subplots(...)`, pass `ax=` to pandas and seaborn, and label axes with units. Save with `dpi` and `bbox_inches="tight"` from a script you can rerun next week, and close each figure in loops.
